discovery: Squeezed states of light and their use to beat the quantum limit of optical measurement
motivation: Caves showed in 1981 that the shot-noise limit of interferometers comes from vacuum fluctuations entering the unused port, and that injecting squeezed vacuum could beat it. This turned a question about the foundations of quantum noise into a design principle for measurement. Kimble's group produced strong, well-characterized squeezing by parametric down-conversion and used it to demonstrate sub-shot-noise measurements. This made squeezed light a controllable quantum resource and opened the field of continuous-variable quantum optics. Schnabel led the work that took squeezing to more than 15 dB and into routine use at GEO600, where it is now a standard part of how the instrument operates. Squeezed light has since become a permanent feature of the LIGO and Virgo detectors, raising their rate of gravitational-wave detections. Together these contributions are a rare complete arc, from theory to a new quantum state of light to measurement capability that has changed what can be observed.
